3.text: outer tent, but they must keep very quiet. The female members of the

4.text: family may stay inside, though it is thought more judicious that there should

5.text: be as few people as possible present. An old woman — a mother or an

6.text: aunt — usually stays with the woman in order to give her a hand in arrang-

8.text: I have spoken before of the tendency of the Chukchee women to reduce

9.text: all assistance at this time to the strictest minimum. Nevertheless, when help

10.text: is necessary, it is given to the woman. I know cases where, in the absence

11.text: of female relatives, the husband has ministered to his wife in her first labors.

12.text: When the child has come into the world, the mother ties up the navel

13.text: with a string of sinew into which a few of her own hairs have been plaited.

14.text: This string, of course, has been prepared beforehand, and kept ready at hand.

15.text: She cuts the navel with a sharp stone, which will serve her for that purpose

16.text: during her whole life. The stone is simply taken from one of the skin-

17.text: scrapers, and ever after that is kept in the clothes-bag of the woman. The

18.text: navel is left unwrapped, but is kept rubbed all the time with dry powdered

19.text: coal, till at last it falls off. The child is rubbed over with urine from the

20.text: mother, which has been kept for the purpose; and the bunch of grass that

21.text: was used in the rubbing is immediately burnt on the hearth.

22.text: With the Reindeer people a young doe is slaughtered, and, in the largest

23.text: kettle of the household, a plentiful supply of strong broth is prepared from

24.text: its brisket. The water or snow for the broth is brought by the husband.

25.text: While filling the kettle, he puts the wooden drum-stick across the upper rim

26.text: of the kettle, and repeats three times a short formula like the following: “O

27.text: Sun! give us warm water.” The woman in child-birth puts a large robe on

28.text: over her bare body, and places under its folds the kettle full of warm broth.

29.text: Over the steam of the broth she warms her breasts, believing that this process

30.text: will make them soften. Then she eats some meat, and drinks of the broth

31.text: as much as she is able to take. She alone must empty the full kettle, and

32.text: the sooner this is done, the better. During the first two weeks she feeds on

33.text: the choicest meat, always carefully boiled, and drinks large quantities of strong

34.text: broth. The broth is considered well adapted to produce a flow of milk into

36.text: Immediately after the delivery, the body of the woman is tightly bound

37.text: around the hips with a cord in order to bring the bones of her body into

38.text: their former position. The Chukchee believe that, without this, the woman

39.text: will become sickly, and that her life will be shortened. The binding must

40.text: not be undone for three days, during which time the woman keeps mostly

41.text: in the inner room, though she may for a short while creep out into the outer

43.text: wife, who is attended only by one or more of her own sex (Captain Ch. F. Hall, Life with the Eskimo, II, p. 313).
